speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It aimed to deliver free civil legal aid to deserving cases.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Ordinance also contained provisions on criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the latter provisions were not brought into force.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That remained the position when we passed the Legal Aid and Advice Act in 1995.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the end, we decided to do so through CLAS – the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme – run by the Law Society.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It allowed more applicants to qualify for criminal legal aid because the funding was supported by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It directed aid to those who needed it most.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, an honorarium was paid to CLAS lawyers, to recognise the contribution of volunteers who will take on criminal legal aid cases.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: However, it has to be said, the honorarium was very nominal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2018 and 2019, we started thinking that we could go further, in providing aid.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We began reviewing our criminal legal aid model.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We engaged the Law Society and the Criminal Bar for their views.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We asked if they would support an expansion of criminal legal aid coverage.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Law Society was, in principle, supportive, as was the criminal bar, but they were concerned about the impact on paid work for lawyers – whether this will take away work from lawyers and whether a lawyer's income will suffer.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They suggested expanding the coverage of offences, instead of increasing the means-test coverage.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They did not want us to cover more people, but they were quite happy to consider whether we can cover more offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After taking in the feedback, we came to our views.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there were a few issues to think about.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, we needed to make sure we try and minimise abuse of the system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I gave examples of this from the United Kingdom and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But you will find it in every jurisdiction.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, to manage costs to ensure fiscal sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One, should we change the model we have and go for a full Government-funded legal aid?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Two, should we give up our public-private sector partnership model in delivering criminal legal aid?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Three, should we expand CLAS beyond the lowest 25% in terms of household income?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We undertook a study of the different criminal legal aid models in other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We looked at 11 jurisdictions: the UK, New Zealand, the two states of New South Wales and Victoria in Australia, the province of Ontario in Canada, Hong Kong, Republic of South Korea, Germany, Japan and the US, at both the New York state level and the federal level.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is not just countries, but also territories.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we looked more closely at six of them, namely, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, New South Wales, Victoria, Ontario and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These six jurisdictions share similar common law traditions and philosophies with Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They aim to provide criminal legal aid to the most vulnerable persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They adopt what is called a judicare model, where the cases are outsourced to the private sector for a fee.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our view is that the Public Defender model has some benefits over the judicare model.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Public Defender Scheme allows development of expertise, because institutional knowledge can be built up.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the judicare model, the assignment of counsel is done ad hoc.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the greater economies of scale which can better help manage costs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And third, our study shows that in the Public Defender model, there is a specialised office – the Public Defender's Office.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over time, it is better able to access expert witnesses, medical, forensic, analysts and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other than Ontario, all the common law jurisdictions we studied adopt a hybrid model.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This means that the state hires in-house lawyers as Public Defenders and also outsources some cases to private lawyers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This model can strengthen the partnership between the private sector and the Government and widen the pool of expertise that can be tapped.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is a model that we are considering.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A strong partnership between the Government and the Criminal Bar is, in my view, quite important.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at the state of Victoria in Australia, for example, the Victorian Bar Association has its own probono scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They offer advice and representation to persons who cannot obtain legal assistance from any other source.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They complement the Public Defenders employed by Victoria Legal Aid.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Singapore, we have had a very strong partnership with the Law Society and the legal fraternity.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have a very strong probono and public spirit and we want to preserve this cooperative relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the Victorian model is one way we can do that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ten of the 11 jurisdictions we studied are fully funded by government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There, the Government co-funds the system with the Law Foundation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Law Foundation is an organisation set up by the legal fraternity.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In any system like this, escalating costs are a major concern where criminal legal aid is fully funded by the state.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I shared an example of escalating costs when I spoke about this in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other jurisdictions also saw similar increases in spending over the last 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After a while, it was no longer sustainable and some of these countries have then had to impose very sudden, drastic cuts to funding.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There were adverse consequences which remain today, including delays in clearing cases.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to learn from these experiences and try to avoid going there and then taking the cutbacks and steps to control costs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we have to structure it in a practical, workable way from the beginning and try and make our criminal legal aid model sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, it is important to structure the Public Defender agency carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The agency can be a part the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, the Public Defenders must be able to carry out their professional duties and defend the recipients of legal aid, where the cases are meritorious.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some jurisdictions have been able to do this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The annex contains examples of abuses of criminal legal aid in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may also access this material through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are two categories of abuses which we need to be aware of.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, some lawyers, not the majority, in other countries overbill, flout the rules, for their own benefit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was a lawyer who billed around S$160,000 between 2013 and 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said this was for travel expenses, meant for cases where the lawyer had to travel more than 200 kilometres to the court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But a check showed that the lawyer's office was actually quite close to the courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to try and first, be aware; and second, avoid this sort of abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Overbilling, in a variety of ways, is not uncommon in these places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, and not infrequently, unmeritorious applicants who take advantage of legal aid include individuals who are asset-rich or wealthy but find ways to meet the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are stories of legal aid recipients who turn up in Rolls Royces and other cars, which they say are not theirs and are held on trust for others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, there are also cases where the applicants fulfil the means and merits tests but are perceived to be morally undeserving of aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There has been an uproar in other jurisdictions when such cases are covered by government-funded aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Victoria, Australia, around S$950,000, nearly a million dollars, was spent to defend a person by the name of Dragan Vasilijkovic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was prosecuted for war crimes during the Yugoslav Wars.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first two categories of abuse, we can try and have systems and frameworks to try and detect and deter such practices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Legal aid cannot depend on public outrage because once we categorise and the means and merits tests are satisfied – merits, means – and I will come to it – we are going to exclude certain types of cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as long as it falls within the categories of cases which would be covered by legal aid, then public outrage, on a case-by-case basis, cannot be the basis on which legal aid is given or not given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will need to think through and explain our position carefully to the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have considered the lessons from others, as well as the feedback from the Law Society and Criminal Bar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government will continue to work with CLAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will also help to preserve the probono spirit of the legal fraternity, which has been a key pillar of legal aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is similar to the Legal Aid Bureau now and the Insolvency and Public Trustee's Office.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be headed by a Chief Public Defender, call him "CPD".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will adopt a hybrid model of criminal legal aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is similar to some of the common law jurisdictions that I spoke about earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It means that the PDO will have full-time lawyers as employees of the PDO and they will take on cases as public defenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PDO will scale up over a period of time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Public Defenders will take on all of PDO's cases in the early years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At a later date, the PDO will begin outsourcing some cases to a panel of qualified lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government will continue to provide some co-funding to CLAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The details of the funding will be assessed and discussed in light of the PDO being set up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other details will also have to be worked out, including the cases which PDO will handle and cases which CLAS will handle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have decided to enhance coverage, both in terms of income and the types of offences covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Currently, CLAS covers up to the 25th percentile of resident households.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This means more needy Singaporeans who require the services of a criminal defence lawyer will be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we will expand the type of offences covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is easier to illustrate that by saying what types of offences will not be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will not be covering regulatory offences such as traffic summonses and departmental charges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will also not be covering offences under nine pieces of legislation whose primary purpose is to deter specific behaviours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are gambling and betting, organised and syndicated crime, and terrorism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offences under these Acts bring about significant negative externalities to society, and public funding, I think, will be difficult to justify being used towards defending such cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: PDO will also have the discretion to exclude cases if the CPD thinks that the representation may not make a material difference to the case’s outcome.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will have to apply a strong merits test approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This includes cases involving offences with established sentencing frameworks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mentioned earlier that we had consulted the Law Society Council and Criminal Bar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were concerned that the expansion of Legal Aid would affect the livelihood of lawyers who were providing paid legal services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of the newly eligible persons who will benefit from expanded coverage, 60% would likely be litigants-in-persons, meaning that the impact on paid work for lawyers should not be substantial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to do the right thing here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our assessment is that in the main, lawyers’ income should not substantially be affected, and their income will not in the main, depend on people at the 35th percentile and below.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Earlier, I spoke about how other jurisdictions have addressed rising costs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also talked about how the system could be abused.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will have to be careful about the cases the Government funds using taxpayers’ money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other jurisdictions, expansions in coverage contributed to higher costs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be staffed by lawyers who handle the work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This can include fresh graduates and younger lawyers, mid-career hires who want to do criminal legal aid work and Legal Service officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These officers will provide the depth of experience and institutional knowledge to build the PDO.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a few questions to the Minister in response to his Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, this is provided that the Bill goes through, but I am quite certain the Ministry would have done some calculation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister covered, generally, three types of legislation: gambling, organised crime and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What other legislation will be excluded for consideration in the event a member of the public seeks assistance from the PDO?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Will there be fundamental differences which would result in a case being handled by one entity as opposed to the other?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Could I ask for the third question again, please?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The third question: Minister covered the legislation that will be excluded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the Minister mentioned nine pieces of legislation will not be under the remit of this department.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister covered three and I am inquiring what the others are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to the questions on how much funding the office is likely to require, the number of staff to begin operations, these are matters of detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have some idea, but I would prefer to deal with it, if necessary, at the Bill stage because there are some discussions going on with the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, maybe the Member can ask him as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not think the Minister for Finance will appreciate me going into those details at this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, I can tell the Member and then, bind the Minister!

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are discussing, both on the staffing and the monetary issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, I am not making a Ministerial Statement here without Cabinet clearance on the principles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we intend to start, as I said, in a very modest way by the end of this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That means trying to get the Bill drafted, put it in place, try to get it put through, have the people employed – all within the next eight months or so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I would prefer to defer the questions on numbers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what the House can be certain about is that, at a steady state, with the kind of framework we are thinking of, a fairly robust means test, merits test, we will cover those who need assistance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to the relationship between PDO and CLAS, again, that is at the margins.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said what we will cover and we will have to discuss with CLAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be perhaps cases which may not qualify for our means test, but CLAS may feel would be good to cover.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, PDO will only assist Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some categories that CLAS may perhaps cover, too, but these are things that will need to be discussed in greater detail with the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I applaud the Government's announcement to set up this Public Defender's Office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a shift from the previous position of the Government not to set up the Public Defender's Office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a good example of how the Government continually looks at policies and makes the necessary changes to suit the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One is in relation to the staffing of the Public Defender's Office with legal officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As this House will note, we had moved amendments in the Constitution to create a Legal Service Commission as well as a Judicial Service Commission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As far as the Public Defender's Office is concerned, may I ask the hon Minister which Commission would be superintending over the officers so that they can be properly developed to be capable in delivering their duties without favour, based on expectations set of them?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second question is in relation to the exclusions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister mentioned about nine statutes which he proposes to exclude.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does he propose to also exclude private prosecution?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because as the hon Minister is aware, there is public prosecution, there is private prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think on the two questions, I will give an answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, first, on the comment on declining PDO, I will stand corrected, I am not sure that we expressly declined to have a PDO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think, in substance, the Member is correct in that the Government has previously taken the position that criminal legal aid ought not to be funded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I described earlier in my Ministerial Statement, by 2013, we explained that we will do so, and we did so through CLAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is a further and very significant step forward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is about nine years now where we have been funding criminal legal aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to the specific questions as to which Commission, I think the right position ought to be that the officers within PDO, qua-PDO, should not be subject to either Commission.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Neither the Judicial Service Commission nor the Legal Service Commission.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will be MinLaw officers, in a department under MinLaw and separate from both Commissions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not, in principle, completely rule out secondments from either Commission.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those are matters of detail which need to be looked at.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when they exercise their duties qua-PDO officers, they will be assessed primarily by MinLaw.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have four clarifications for the Minister for Law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, I would like his confirmation that the setting up of PDO in no way affects the current High Court scheme for the Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences (LASCO).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Meaning that the scheme for legal representation of capital cases still remains within the province of the Supreme Court and this scheme in no way changes that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second question, the Minister mentioned earlier that the demarcation of work between PDO and CLAS would be worked out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder whether he could comment on whether certain statutes are currently not covered by CLAS – for example, road traffic offences – whether there has been discussion that PDO could accept some of these cases, which tend to affect the people of lower-income.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I mean, it stretches the strata of society, so there will be a significant section of the public who would benefit from coverage under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The third question, on excluded offences again, the Minister mentioned that there might be certain offences not covered because there is some moral reprehensibility about them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder whether it might also include, for example, drink driving cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would the Minister be able to comment on that specifically?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And last of all, my question is whether the PDO scheme would also handle appeals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first question on LASCO, I actually did not touch on LASCO at all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is something that we need to discuss with the Supreme Court, what makes sense from a public taxpayer's perspective and the perspective of the person to be defended, and the institutions involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these are issues that need to be discussed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On demarcation of work between PDO and CLAS, as I had indicated to the Leader of the Opposition, this is something that needs to be discussed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Road traffic offences can fall in different categories.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some may be regulatory, some will be much more than regulatory.
